excerpt: Why there is no reliable "average" personal injury settlement, what the most recent federal court data shows, and the factors that actually drive case value in Georgia and South Carolina.
keyTakeaways: There is no reliable "average" settlement. In the most recent federal study of state-court tort trials (Bureau of Justice Statistics, 2005 data), half of winning plaintiffs were awarded $24,000 or less ($15,000 in car-accident trials, $400,000 in medical-malpractice trials), but those are trial awards, not settlements. Only about 4% of tort cases end in a trial; most of the rest settle. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1). South Carolina caps them at the greater of 3x compensatory damages or an inflation-indexed $500,000, which is $739,245 in 2026 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530); the cap rises to the greater of 4x or $2 million for certain profit-motivated misconduct or conduct that could support a felony conviction, and does not apply to impaired defendants, intent to harm, or a felony plea or conviction for the same conduct.

faqs.question: What is the average personal injury settlement?
faqs.answer: There is no reliable national average for settlements, because insurers do not publish them and every case turns on its own injuries, evidence and insurance. The closest federal data are trial verdicts: in the Bureau of Justice Statistics' most recent study (2005 data), half of plaintiffs who won a tort trial in state court were awarded $24,000 or less, with a median of $15,000 in car-accident trials and $400,000 in medical-malpractice trials. An attorney who reviews your records can give you a realistic range.

faqs.question: Why do amounts vary so much?
faqs.answer: Key variables include injury severity, medical costs, lost income, permanent impairment, liability clarity, available insurance, jurisdiction, and attorney skill.

faqs.question: Do most cases settle or go to trial?
faqs.answer: Most settle. In the most recent Bureau of Justice Statistics count (2005 data), only about 4% of tort cases in state courts ended in a trial. An attorney who is prepared to try your case gives the insurer a real reason to make a fair offer.

faqs.question: How long to receive a settlement?
faqs.answer: It depends on your treatment and the insurer. Most claims are not ready to settle until your treatment reaches maximum medical improvement, and cases that go into litigation take longer. The filing deadlines do not wait: two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).

faqs.question: Are settlements taxable?
faqs.answer: Compensation for physical injuries is generally not taxable. Punitive damages and interest are taxable.

faqs.question: How can I get a realistic estimate?
faqs.answer: Free consultation with an experienced attorney who can review records, calculate damages, and provide a range based on comparable cases.
